clinicalPearls: Bleeding into the loose potential space between the scalp aponeurosis and the periosteum, which can hold a large volume of blood
It is the most dangerous of the extracranial birth haemorrhages because it can cause life-threatening blood loss
It is strongly associated with vacuum-assisted (and sometimes forceps) delivery
The swelling is diffuse, boggy and fluctuant, crosses sutures and may shift with position, sometimes with a fluid thrill
Signs of hypovolaemia (tachycardia, pallor, falling haematocrit) and expanding head circumference indicate ongoing bleeding
Management requires close monitoring, volume and blood-product resuscitation and correction of coagulopathy
reference.pathophysiology: Subgaleal haemorrhage occurs when shearing forces, characteristically from vacuum extraction, rupture the emissary veins traversing the subgaleal space. Because this space is large and unconfined by suture attachments, it can accommodate a substantial proportion of the neonate's blood volume, leading to significant, sometimes catastrophic, haemorrhage. The resulting hypovolaemia and any accompanying coagulopathy can cause shock, and breakdown of the extravasated blood contributes to jaundice.
additionalInvestigations: Serial head circumference measurement and clinical assessment of the swelling
Full blood count and serial haematocrit
Continuous vital sign monitoring for hypovolaemia
redFlags: Expanding swelling with rising head circumference
Tachycardia, pallor or falling haematocrit indicating significant blood loss
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and aggressive resuscitation most infants recover, but delayed diagnosis of a large or ongoing bleed can be fatal; the condition demands vigilance after assisted delivery.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for benign caput succedaneum and underestimating blood loss
Failing to monitor head circumference and haematocrit serially
management: Recognise early and admit to neonatal intensive care with continuous monitoring of heart rate, blood pressure and perfusion
Restore circulating volume with crystalloid and transfuse packed red cells for significant blood loss and anaemia
Correct coagulopathy with fresh frozen plasma, platelets and vitamin K as required
Track ongoing bleeding with serial head circumference measurement and serial haematocrit
Monitor and treat hyperbilirubinaemia with phototherapy, or exchange transfusion if severe, as the collection resorbs
Escalate to intensive support for hypovolaemic shock or disseminated intravascular coagulation
Image the cranium when an associated skull fracture or intracranial injury is suspected
